text: I shoot every day of my life on a pocket camera. A month in the US, a hundred and sixty clips a week. Editing one day used to take me a whole night. For a month I edited with an AI agent in the terminal, and wrote down every correction I gave it. This is that agent as a product: Life2Film Director, a personal film director that knows my footage and my taste.

Everything lives in Neon Postgres. Nine days of footage, six hundred and forty-eight clips, five and a half thousand sentences with word timings, nine thousand scored shots, and a caption of what the camera saw in every clip. Search is hybrid: Lakebase vector search plus BM25, fused with reciprocal rank. Ask where my daughter talks about home, and it returns the clip, the second, and the line. Ask for a sunset by the ocean, and it finds the picture even when nobody spoke.

Then the director writes the script. It reads the whole day as text and my ten standing rules, learned from a month of my own corrections: open with a hook, never cut a thought mid-sentence, show what is being talked about. The script is validated against the footage, laid out as OpenTimelineIO, and rendered by my open-source Rust renderer on the Mac. On Fly it would be a sprite. This is the family reel it cut for my mother, from search results, in under four minutes.

And it learns. I said: the first ten seconds are boring, I need a hook, fire, water, faces. That remark became a durable rule in Neon, the script was revised, the opening re-cut. Next film, same taste, no repeat. New clips need no pre-processing: the life2film engine scores frames in WebAssembly, whisper transcribes, a vision model captions, and clips mailed from my phone to the agent's own AgentMail inbox become footage automatically.

For parents, it is a family archive you can ask questions and get a reel for grandma. For vloggers, the daily cut without the editing night. Mastra agent, assistant-ui, Neon with Lakebase Search, AgentMail, Exa for the facts, and it is open source under MIT. Thank you.
